The call chain is:
- `UsersService.findOne` (`users/users.service.ts:21`) is called by `AuthService.signIn` (`auth/auth.service.ts:13`).
- `AuthService.signIn` is called by `AuthController`, at the `@Public() @Post('login')` handler (`auth/auth.controller.ts:19-21`).

`findOne` has no other callers in `src`, apart from the unit test setup in `users.service.spec.ts`. `UsersModule` exports `UsersService`, but only `AuthService` injects it.

**`GET /auth/profile`** is not affected. It is in the same controller, but it doesn't call `AuthService` or `UsersService`. The JWT guard that protects it only verifies the token, so it doesn't call `findOne` either.

If `findOne` changes its return shape (`User | undefined`, including the `password`, `userId` and `username` fields), `signIn` is what would break. It compares `user?.password` to the submitted password and builds the JWT payload from `user.username` and `user.userId`. A change there would alter the login response and the contents of the issued token. Every protected route reads that token's payload, so those routes would see the difference indirectly. That is a change in the token's contents, not a code dependency on `findOne`.

`app.listen` is implemented in `lib/application.js:598`.

It creates a plain Node.js HTTP server with `http.createServer(this)`, where `this` is the Express app. The app is itself a request-handler function, so it serves as the server's request listener. The method then calls `server.listen(...)` with the arguments you passed. It does not create an HTTPS server. For HTTPS you would build the server yourself with `https.createServer(options, app)`.

If the last argument is a callback, `listen` wraps it in `once` and also attaches it as a one-time `error` handler on the server. I only read the first few lines of the function, so I haven't checked what happens after that.

`app.listen` is implemented in `lib/application.js` at line 598.

It creates a plain Node.js HTTP server with `http.createServer(this)`. The Express app (`this`) is passed in as the request handler. It then calls `server.listen` with the arguments you gave it.

If the last argument is a callback, it is wrapped in `once` and also attached to the server's `error` event. That way the callback runs once, whether the server starts or fails to start.

It does not create an HTTPS server. For HTTPS you create the server yourself with `https.createServer(options, app)`.
